sections.title: When Faith and Politics Meet
sections.description:
Debates about whether, when, and how religion should shape politics and politics should shape religion are older than this republic. The political polarization defining these debates isn’t new either, but unlike in other contentious disagreements – about gun control, for instance – injecting faith into the conversation is by its nature more resolute.
It is challenging to argue about one’s God, or one’s disbelief in a God, and how that divinity operates (or doesn’t) in our daily lives. Many of us were raised in households where religious attachment and voting patterns were so intertwined that they became indistinguishable. The Catholics who mounted photos of President Kennedy on their walls. The Christian evangelicals who prayed with President Trump. And more recently, the Muslims who joyfully welcomed Zohran Mamdani’s victory in New York City.
In this seminar, first-year students will encounter faith teachings from their foundational texts to modern interpretations, and will explore how America’s various traditions shape and are shaped by our political behavior. We will focus on three overarching questions:
When does life begin, when does it end, and who decides?
Who belongs in a community, who does not, and how is that enforced?
Where is the line between state power and religious autonomy?
The goal of this course is not to proselytize, criticize, or demonize; nor is it to turn away from material too toxic to touch. Students will be obliged to understand views antithetical to their own, and robustly argue for or against them in conversations that may be unsettling and challenging. This will encourage them to cultivate a deep awareness of and nuanced appreciation for America’s ongoing experiment in crafting a society where political and religious disagreements can tolerate and enrich each other.
